t: and they make pilgrimage to it three times a year. They come to this house on the three festivals and offer sacrifices there (see Hilchot Chagigah 1:1).
and the Torah already detailed the Tabernacle that Moses our teacher made. In the book of Exodus from the portion of Terumah to the end of the book.
and it was for the moment. It served as a sanctuary only temporarily.

for you have not yet come. The verse continues: "to the rest and to the inheritance." After they inherit the land and rest from their enemies, they will build a Temple at "the place that the Lord shall choose" and bring their offerings there (Deuteronomy chapter 12; and see Hilchot Melakhim 1:1-2).

and they came to Nob and built a Temple there... and they came to Gibeon and built a Temple there. In these places they erected the Tent of Meeting that had been made in the wilderness (Peirush HaMishnayot, Zevachim 14:7; Arukh HaShulchan 1:17).
to the House of Eternity. To the Temple in Jerusalem.

all the places were forbidden to build in them a house for the Lord and to offer a sacrifice in them. While the Tabernacle was at Gilgal and in the days of Nob and Gibeon it was permitted to build private altars anywhere and offer sacrifices on them (Mishnah Zevachim 14:4-8).
and there is no house there for all generations, etc.. One may never build a house except in Jerusalem.

and on Mount Moriah, in it, as it is said: "And David said, 'This is the house of the Lord God'". After he built an altar at the threshing floor of Ornan and the Lord appeared to him in fire. And this place was on Mount Moriah (II Chronicles 3:1; and see below 2:1-2).
forever. In the preceding verse it says: "For the Lord has chosen Zion; He has desired it for His habitation."
explained in Kings. I Kings chapters 6-7.
written in Ezekiel. Chapters 40-44.
when they built it in the days of Ezra. As described in the book of Ezra.
things that are essential. Things that are indispensable.
and all three are called the Heikhal. Sometimes this term refers only to the Holy and the Holy of Holies, or to the Holy alone (for example, below 3:17, 7:21).
like the hangings of the courtyard that were in the wilderness. This partition corresponds to the partition of the Tabernacle courtyard.
the altar for the burnt offering. This is how this altar is sometimes called in the Torah (Exodus 30:28 and elsewhere).
and the ramp by which one ascends to the altar. A sloping ascent from which they went up to the top of the altar.
and its place is before the Ulam, drawn toward the south. The altar and the ramp stood in the courtyard east of the Ulam on its southern side (see below 5:14-16).
and its base. A foundation for the laver.
for the priests to sanctify from it their hands and their feet for the service. To wash their hands and feet with water before beginning the service (see Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 5:1).
which is to the left of one entering the Temple. For one entering the Temple enters from east to west.
and all three are inside the Holy, before the Holy of Holies. In the inner third of the Holy (below 3:17).
drawn from between the two outward. Toward the east.
and they make boundaries within the courtyard, etc.. The courtyard was divided into various areas, and each area was defined by who was permitted to enter it (below 5:12).
and they build in it rooms for the other needs of the Temple. The details of their locations and purposes are given below 5:7-10 and there in halakhah 17.
bricks. Building blocks made of clay.
they split the building stones. They divide a large stone into two stones.

as it is said: "great stones, etc.". "And the king commanded, and they quarried great stones... to lay the foundation of the house, hewn stones," from which we learn that they dressed the stones outside and afterwards moved them to the Temple Mount.
and they do not build into it any projecting wood at all. This law derives from the prohibition against planting a tree beside the altar and in the courtyard (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 6:9-10).
porticos. A roofed structure made of wood.
and it is forbidden for the priest performing the service to stand on it during the service, etc.. For during the service he must stand on the courtyard floor (see Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 5:17-19).
and to assist. To help.
like the Temple of the wilderness. As was done in building the Tabernacle (see Exodus 35:4-36:8).
and they do not interrupt the schoolchildren. From their studies (see also Hilchot Talmud Torah 2:2).
arches. A structure of arches that creates a space between the ground and what is above it (compare below 5:1).
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

for it is not optional but obligatory. The word "if" in the verse "And if you make Me an altar of stones" is interpreted as obligatory: that one must build a permanent altar (unlike in the Tabernacle) and that it be made of stones.
that is nicked so that a fingernail catches on it. So that if one runs a fingernail over its surface, it catches on the nick.
like a slaughtering knife. Similar to the measure of nick that disqualifies a slaughtering knife (see Hilchot Shechitah 1, halakhot 14, 23).

and from where did they bring the stones of the altar. Which had not been nicked and which iron had never touched (as explained below in halakhah 15; for how the altar was built from these stones see below 2:16).
from virgin ground. Ground that had never been worked.
and likewise the stones of the Heikhal and the courtyards were whole. Smooth, without nicks (though they could be split and dressed, as above in halakhah 8).
that were damaged. Broken and cut.
and they have no redemption but are put away. They cannot be redeemed and made ordinary for use, and so they are stored away.

any stone that iron touched... is disqualified for the construction of the altar. Because iron was created to shorten a person's days, and the altar was created to lengthen a person's days (Mishnah Middot 3:4). Therefore the stones of the altar are not dressed.

and one who builds with a nicked stone transgresses a positive commandment. Learned from the verse "You shall build with whole stones" (Kesef Mishneh; and see Radbaz and Mishneh LaMelekh, who discussed the nature of this prohibition).
and they whitewash. They plaster with lime (Riko). Some explain: they clean (Rabbi Y. Kafah).
with an iron trowel. A piece of iron with which the builders smooth the stones of the walls.
one who demolishes. Breaks down.
in a destructive manner. But it is permitted to demolish in order to repair.

"And you shall tear down their altars, etc. You shall not do so to the Lord your God". The verse instructs us to break down the altars of idolatry, and forbids doing so to the Lord (see also Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:7).
the service vessels. Vessels used for the holy service in the Temple (see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:13).
the basins. In which they received the blood that was thrown on the altar.
and the spits and the shovels of the altar of the burnt offering. Iron pipes and shovels with which they cleaned the altar.
and the measures. Measuring vessels (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:16-17).
and vessels of height. Vessels made for the sake of the Most High, for the sake of the sanctity of God.
stones and beams that he hewed originally for a synagogue, etc.. Although they were hewn for a holy purpose, they were not hewn for the sanctity of the Temple Mount.
as it is said: "And this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel". So said King David after he bought the site of the Temple from Araunah the Jebusite and built an altar there.

and it says: "And Solomon built the house on Mount Moriah". This combines two verses: in Kings it says "And Solomon built the house and finished it," and in Chronicles it says "And Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah."
that Noah built on it. An altar, on which he offered burnt offerings (Genesis 8:20).
and it is the altar on which Cain and Abel offered. Genesis 4:3-4.
and on it Adam the first man offered a sacrifice when he was created. According to the words of the Sages (Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 8a and elsewhere).
Adam was created from the place of his atonement. The place from which the Holy One took the earth to form Adam was the place of the altar, which is what atones for a person (Bereishit Rabbah 14:8).
the measurements of the altar are exact. Its dimensions must be precise.

and the altar that the returnees from exile built, they made like the altar that is destined to be built. Those returning from the Babylonian exile who built the altar in the Second Temple enlarged its dimensions relative to Solomon's altar (Mishnah Middot 3:1), and they did so according to the dimensions of the altar that will be built in the Third Temple.
and not to reduce from it. Ideally, but after the fact it is valid (as explained below in halakhah 17, by way of wisdom).
and three prophets. Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Rashi, Zevachim 62a).
that one offers sacrifices on this altar, etc.. When the altar exists and stands in its place, sacrifices may be offered even when the Temple is not built (see below 6:15).
that Moses made. In the Tabernacle.
and that Solomon made. In the First Temple.

its height three cubits, the place of the arrangement only. The altar was built in three sections (as in halakhah 7 below); the fire arrangement on which the offerings were offered was at the top of its upper section, and this section was three cubits high.

some by a cubit of five handbreadths and some by a cubit of six handbreadths. In all of the Torah's length measurements, the cubit is six handbreadths (Hilchot Shabbat 17:36). But regarding the altar there is a tradition that parts of it are measured in cubits of five handbreadths (the base cubit, the horns' cubit, and the cubits of the golden altar - Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 3:1).
and the height of the entire altar is fifty-eight handbreadths. Two of the ten cubits were of five handbreadths, so in total there were fifty-eight handbreadths.

and this was its measure and form. The basic shape of the altar is three cubes placed one upon the other. The lower part of the altar is a square of thirty-two cubits, called the "yesod" (base). Above it is the "sovev" (surround), which is smaller than the base by five handbreadths on each side. Above the sovev was another square, the "place of the arrangement," on which they arranged the fires and offered the sacrifices. The square of the "place of the arrangement" is smaller than the sovev by five handbreadths on each side.
this is the sovev. It is called this because, unlike the base, it surrounded the altar on all its sides (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 3:2).

and the place of the horns, a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side all around. At the four corners of the top of the "place of the arrangement" were horns. The horns were a regular cubit (six handbreadths) in length and width, and a small cubit (five handbreadths) in height. Opposite that cubit all around (the area between horn and horn) they did not use.

and likewise the place of the priests' feet, a cubit all around. Inward from the place of the horns, on all sides of the altar they left another cubit unused, so that the priests could walk and stand there.
so the place of the arrangement is twenty-four cubits and four handbreadths wide, etc.. The rest of the area at the top of the altar served for the fires on which sacrifices were offered.
and the square of each horn. The square of each horn, its length and width.
and the four horns were hollow inside. Below, in halakhah 16, it is explained how the hollows were made.
and the height of the place of the arrangement is eighteen handbreadths. From the sovev to the top of the altar.

so half the height of the altar is six handbreadths below the end of the sovev. The sovev was thirty-five handbreadths high from the ground and the height of the entire altar was fifty-eight handbreadths, so half the height is six handbreadths (a cubit) below the sovev.
and a line of red dye, etc.. A red line went around the altar on all its sides.

to separate between the upper blood and the lower blood. Some offerings have their blood applied on the upper part of the altar (such as a sin offering), and some have their blood applied on the lower part of the altar (such as a burnt offering).
nine cubits less a handbreadth. This is the height of the altar without the horns, taking into account that the base cubit is five handbreadths.

and in the southwestern horn there were two holes, etc.. They poured the remainder of the blood on the southern and western base, and therefore they made holes in the southwestern corner so that the blood would drain through them (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 3:2).

and they mix in the amah and go out to the Kidron stream. From the pits the blood flowed into a water channel in the courtyard floor (the "amah") and from it went out to the Kidron stream, where they collected the blood and sold it as fertilizer (Hilchot Me'ilah 2:11).
and a marble slab and a ring fixed in it. That spot was covered with a marble slab that was lifted by an iron ring.

by which they go down to the pit and clean it. From that spot they would go down to clean a place underground called the "shit." The wines of the libations gathered there through two holes descending from the altar.
and this is its form. In the diagram here the altar is shown from above.

and it consumed thirty cubits in the ground, etc.. Thirty of the thirty-two cubits of the ramp's length lay on the ground. Another cubit was slightly higher than the rest of the ramp and rose above the place of the base, and the last cubit was higher still and rose above the sovev.

in order to place the limbs by throwing. The limbs of the offerings must be thrown onto the altar from its side, similar to the throwing of the blood (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:4). Therefore they separated the ramp from the altar so that throwing from there would count as throwing from the side of the altar.
nine cubits less a sixth. Less a handbreadth (which is a sixth of a cubit), so that the ramp was aligned with the height of the arrangement (see halakhah 9 above).
as the thickness of a thread. The width of a hair.
and a window. A niche.

in which they put the disqualified bird sin offerings, etc.. When a bird sin offering was disqualified in a way that it could not be burned immediately (for example, disqualified through doubt), they would throw it into the rovovah until it spoiled and could be burned.
to the place of burning. A place in the courtyard where they burned offerings that had been disqualified (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
on which they put the limbs. Of the offerings that were to be offered on the altar, before taking them up the ramp. They were made of marble and not gold to prevent heating and spoiling of the meat.
and one of silver on which they put the service vessels. The ninety-three service vessels needed for the Temple's services each day (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bertinoro, Shekalim 6:4).
kunya. Lead dross.

and he melts and pours into a large mold according to its measure. He would melt all the materials together and pour them, along with stones, into molds the size of the altar's cubes. At each stage they poured one cube: first into a square the dimensions of the base, then above it they poured into a square of the dimensions of the sovev, and above that into a square of the dimensions of the place of the arrangement.

and places inside the structure a body of wood or stone, etc.. So that the altar structure would be complete and precise, they would place inside the mold wood or stone in a place that was to be empty of base. After the base dried, they removed them, and the altar remained complete and precise. In the same way they made the horns hollow: they placed wood or stone in the casting and a hollow was formed.
and its base and its squareness. That it have a base and that it be built in an exact square.

like the measure of the place of the arrangement of the wilderness altar. Whose height was three cubits (as in halakhah 5 above), and whose area was five cubits square (Exodus 27:1), from which a cubit on each side was subtracted for the horns and a cubit for the priests' walking, leaving the place of the arrangement a total of one cubit.
an altar that was damaged in its structure. Some of its plaster was lost.
provided that there is not among the remainder a nicked stone. For a nicked stone is disqualified even by a fingernail catching (above 1:14).
its form is explained in the Torah. Exodus 25:31-40.
in the shaft of the menorah. The middle shaft (which is called simply "the menorah").
its knobs and its flowers. And the minimum of plural is two.
to its thigh. The base of the menorah, its foundation.
and it had three feet. To its thigh.

and everything is almond-shaped, almond-shaped, in its making. All the cups, knobs and flowers were of almond work, which is the making of almond-like shapes in metal by hammering with a chisel (Peirush HaMishnayot, Menachot 3:7).

of pure gold it shall be, all of it one talent, with its lamps, etc.. The Torah says to make the menorah weighing a talent of gold, and also says that it is to be made "of one piece" - from a single piece of gold shaped into a menorah, not from several pieces joined together. These stringencies were said specifically when the menorah is made of gold.
talent. Sixty maneh, which are one thousand five hundred holy shekels (about forty-two and a half kg).
of one piece, from the beaten work. One mass of metal.
and if it was hollow it is valid. If it was made from one mass even though it has hollows (like tubes) it is valid.
but of other kinds of metal. The menorah should ideally be made of gold; if they could not make it of gold, it may be made of other kinds of metal, but not of other materials (above 1:18).
the scraps. Broken vessels and pieces of metal.
the tongs. With which they removed the wicks from the lamp.
and the fire-pans. Spoons used for removing the ash left in the lamp.
its lamps. The receptacles at the top of the menorah in which the oil and wick burn.
and all the lamps are fixed to the branches. Attached to them, and not detachable.
all of them face the middle lamp on the shaft of the menorah. The mouths of the lamps and the wicks in them faced toward the center of the menorah, toward the middle lamp.
and it is called the western lamp. Because it faces the Holy of Holies, which is west of the menorah.
the cups are like Alexandrian goblets, etc.. Cone-shaped cups with a wide mouth and narrow bottom.

like Beirut apples, etc.. There are versions: "Beiruti" or "Beirutim," and according to this it seems to mean apples from the city of Beirut in Lebanon, and this may also be the meaning according to the printed text, but it is possible, if vocalized differently, that it means wild apples (note of R. Y. Shilat in Rambam Meduyak). Some explain that it means apples of a tree called "berot" or "brosh" (and they disagreed on the identification of this tree).
that are somewhat elongated like an egg both of whose ends are alike. That they are not perfectly round but elongated like an egg whose two ends are not pointed.
the flowers of the pillars, etc.. The capital of a column with a lip folded outward.
on which a priest stands. Since the height of the menorah was eighteen handbreadths, the priest had to stand in a high place to reach the lamps.
and tends the lamps. He cleans the lamps that went out, replaces their wicks, and lights them (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:12; for other opinions see the Pesakim VeShitot there).
along the length of the house. From east to west.
along the width of the house. From north to south.
the lamps of the arrangement. The lamps of the menorah.

four golden supports, etc.. The twelve loaves of the showbread were arranged in two stacks ("arrangements," "rows") on the table. In each were six loaves placed one upon the other (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:2). At the sides of the stacks were posts that branched at the top in a Y shape (Peirush HaMishnayot, Menachot 11:6), on which they rested the stacks.
and the two bowls in which they put the frankincense. Beside the showbread they placed on the table two vessels containing frankincense (see also Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:2).
and the molds. Forms.

and two tables were in the Ulam on the inside, etc.. On the table inside the Heikhal there always had to be bread. Every Shabbat they replaced the loaves. The new bread was placed before bringing it in on a marble table that was in the Ulam near the entrance to the Heikhal. After the bread that had been in the Heikhal was taken out, it was placed on a gold table that was in the Ulam, and afterwards it was distributed to the priests (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:4-5).
a cubit by a cubit. In a cubit of five handbreadths (Peirush HaMishnayot, Kelim 17:10; and see above 2:6).
aligned between the north and the south. Exactly in the middle.
drawn from between the table and the menorah outward. East of the table and the menorah.
from the third of the Heikhal inward. In the western part of the Heikhal.
twelve spigots. Twelve outlets for water.

so that all the priests engaged in the Tamid could sanctify from it at once. For in the second lottery, to determine which priests would perform the daily services of the Temple, thirteen priests were chosen (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 4:6), and all of them except the slaughterer (see Peirush HaMishnayot, Yoma 3:10) had to prepare for the service by washing hands and feet immediately after the lottery.
and they made a mukhni for it, etc.. A vessel that stood above the laver and from which water came out as needed into the laver (compare Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 5:14-15).

and it is non-sacred, so that the water in it would not be disqualified by being left overnight. Unlike the laver, which was a sacred vessel, the mukhni was not consecrated, so that the water placed in it would not be disqualified by lodging if the night passed over it.
there was a stone in the Holy of Holies on its western side. This is the "Foundation Stone" (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:1 and the commentary there).
the jar of manna. In which they filled an omer of manna as a memorial (Exodus 16:33).
and Aaron's staff. The staff of Aaron the priest, which blossomed and testified that Aaron was chosen for the high priesthood (Numbers 17:16-26).

"Put the holy ark in the house". According to the Sages the verse is explained to mean that the ark is to be hidden in the place that King Solomon prepared, and after they hide it they will no longer have the duty of carrying, but only the duties of song and locking the gates.
and the anointing oil. With which they anointed and sanctified the vessels of the Tabernacle, the high priests, and more (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:1-12).

the Urim and Tummim. According to Maimonides this refers to the stones of the breastplate on which the names of the tribes of Israel were engraved, and through them they would ask the high priest and receive answers by divine inspiration (see ibid. 10:10-11 and the Pesakim VeShitot there).
so that there would be no lack of garments. For a priest who served without all the priestly garments, his service is invalid (ibid. 10:4).
a wall separating the Holy and the Holy of Holies, its thickness a cubit. This wall is called the "Tarksin" and had an opening over which hung a curtain (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 4:7).

they were in doubt whether the thickness of the wall belonged to the measure of the Holy or to the measure of the Holy of Holies. The curtain separating the Holy from the Holy of Holies was attached to the wall on the outside. However it was not known whether the wall stood in the twentieth cubit or the twenty-first cubit from the western wall of the Holy of Holies.
the Heikhal that the returnees from exile built, etc.. Its dimensions were greater than those of the First Temple that Solomon built (see I Kings 6:2-3).
height. Elevation.
solid and sealed, like a foundation for it. A foundation for the building on which they built the walls.
the carving in the ceiling. The ceiling of the Heikhal was a cubit thick, and designs were made in it by carving and engraving in plaster and stones.
two cubits of empty space to let the leakage through. Above the ceiling they left an empty space through which water that leaked from above drained out.
the ceiling over the beit dilfa. Wooden beams.
and the ma'aziva. Lime and stones that covered the beams.
and an upper story built over it, the height of its walls forty cubits. A second story that the Heikhal had.
and the height of the parapet. That was above the upper ceiling.
and an iron plate like a sword. A sharp iron plate like a blade.
that drives off ravens. It eliminates (scares away) the ravens.
four walls, one inside the other, and between them three empty spaces. West of the Heikhal there were four walls standing one behind the other with spaces between them.

and the walls of the Holy were six walls, one inside the other, and between them five empty spaces. These spaces were built in three stories and were called "cells" (below in halakhah 10, and see the diagram below on p. 34 for what the various spaces were called and what they were used for).
and the Heikhal had two wickets. See the diagram below on p. 34.
the great gate. The entrance to the Heikhal on the east side.

and he walks between the two walls, etc.. When they opened the doors of the Heikhal in the morning, they walked between the walls north of the Heikhal (for there were spaces between the walls) and turned left toward the Heikhal at the opening in its northern wall (see the illustration below in halakhah 8), from there they turned toward the Heikhal gate and opened it from the inside.
the great gate. The gate of the Heikhal.

two inside and two outside. The thickness of the gateway was six cubits, the width of the Heikhal wall (above in halakhah 4). On each side it had two doors, each five cubits, to close half of the width of the opening.
the outer ones open into the doorway to cover the thickness of the wall. The outer doors covered five cubits of the thickness of the wall, which was six cubits.

and the inner ones open into the house to cover the backs of the doors. The inner doors opened fully until their back part covered the inner side of the Heikhal wall. For the areas behind the doors were not overlaid with gold (Mishnah Middot 4:1).
and five lintels. Beams carved and fashioned in forms and images.
mela. A kind of wood, or the name of the design carved on the wood (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 3:7).

and each of the five extends beyond the one below it by a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side. And they likewise extended in the width of the beam, thereby creating a kind of dome above the opening (Peirush HaMishnayot, ibid.).
and a course of stones. A row of stones.

the building of the Heikhal was wide in front and narrow at the back. Although the Heikhal as a whole was one hundred by one hundred cubits, they narrowed the building slightly so that the western side was a bit narrower than the eastern side (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 4:7).
like a lion. Whose front is broader than its back.

and there were ledges surrounding the entire house all around. Outside the outer wall of the Heikhal were built projections that surrounded the wall along its whole length. The ledges were built in three stories. The lower ledge was narrower than the one above it, and the middle one was narrower than the upper one. This structure prevented climbing the walls of the Heikhal from outside (Peirush HaMishnayot, ibid. 4:4).

the lower ledge five and the rovad above it six. The width of the ledge was five cubits and at its top was a row of stones wider, six cubits in width (Mount Moriah, based on Maimonides' diagram in Peirush HaMishnayot there).
they surround the house on three sides. North, west and south.

one cubit plain and the rovad three cubits. Along the whole length of the wall there was one cubit of wall of regular width, and above it a projection in the building three cubits high, and so on up to the top of the wall. The uppermost projection at the top of the wall was four cubits high.
five on the north and five on the south. The spaces between the six walls that were on the north and south.
and three on the west. The spaces between the four walls that were on the west.
and there were three stories. The cells were built in three stories.
and two on top of them in one story. In the uppermost story of cells there were only two cells (in this part of the height there were only three walls).
each had three openings, etc.. Except for the upper cells, which had no opening above, and the end cells, which had an opening only from their inner side.

and in the northeast corner, in the cell on the middle story, there were five openings. The commentators found this halakhah difficult and offered many explanations of it (see Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 4:3 and the commentators on the Mishnah and Maimonides). It may be explained that this refers to the middle story, to the cell adjacent to the Heikhal on the north, which was divided into two parts because of the passage into the Heikhal that was in its middle. This cell had five openings: one to the cell above; one to the cell below, called the mesibah (or through which one reached the mesibah); one to the left through which one enters the Heikhal; and on the right were two openings: one on its eastern side ("to the cell with the wicket") and one on its western side ("to the cell on the right").
and a mesibah went up, etc.. Within the cells surrounding the Heikhal was a path by which they ascended to the roofs of the cells.

he would go up the mesibah with his face to the west, etc.. To reach the upper story of the Heikhal they would go up the mesibah and continue circling the entire Heikhal to the opening of the ascent, which was in the southeast.
two cedar poles by which they go up to the roof of the upper story. A ladder made of two long beams used to ascend to the Heikhal.
and tops of partitions. A small perforated partition made of reeds, wood or stones.
and openings. Hatches.

through which they lower the craftsmen in boxes, etc.. Although it is forbidden to enter the Holy of Holies except for the high priest on Yom Kippur (below 7:22), it is permitted to enter there to repair and whitewash. They would lower the craftsmen in closed boxes so that they would not look at the Holy of Holies (see below 7:23).
they whitewash. They plaster with lime.

and arches upon arches were built beneath it, etc.. The Temple Mount stood on two stories of arches built so that the two legs of the arches in the upper story stood on the roof of the arches in the lower story. In this way there was everywhere a space that interrupted and separated between ground impurity and the Temple Mount (see Hilchot Parah 3:1).
and all of it was roofed. The entire perimeter of the Temple Mount.
portico within portico. A double row of columns on which the roofing rested.
within it. From the wall of the Temple Mount.
soreg. A partition made as a lattice.
the chel and the wall. A small wall (the chel), and a large wall (the wall of the courtyard).
and this gate is called the Upper Gate. It is called this because it was higher (by fifteen steps) than the Women's Courtyard (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:6).
and it is called the Nicanor Gate. After the man who donated its doors (for the story see Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 38a).
the Women's Courtyard. Called this because women would not usually enter beyond it.
its corners. Its corners.

and they were not roofed, and so they will be in the future. As it says in Ezekiel's prophecy that the chambers in the corners of the Women's Courtyard will be "enclosed" (Ezekiel 46:22), meaning without a ceiling.

for there they cook their peace offerings and shave their hair. The nazir would throw his hair into the fire beneath the pot in which the ram of peace offering that he brought at the end of his naziriteship was cooked (Hilchot Nezirut 8:2-3).
for there priests with blemishes pick wood for worms. They remove the wormy wood, and since priests with blemishes are disqualified from the service of the offerings, they were given this work.
for any wood in which a worm is found is disqualified. For the fires on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:2).
the Chamber of the Lepers. There the lepers immersed when they came to the Temple to bring their offerings (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:1).
wine and oil. For the meal offerings and the libations.

surrounded by a gallery so that the women could see, etc.. In the Women's Courtyard they held the celebration of the water drawing, with the participation of men and women, and to prevent their mingling together, they made around the Women's Courtyard raised galleries on columns on which the women stood (see Mishnah Sukkah 5:1 and Peirush HaMishnayot there).
and it was built as a dome. A rounded ceiling.
and surrounded by stone ledges. Stone benches on which the elder priests would sleep (see Mishnah Tamid 1:1).
two are holy. The two southern chambers that faced the courtyard were holy with the holiness of the courtyard.
and tops of partitions. A small perforated partition made of reeds or wood or stones.
the Chamber of the Lambs. In it were lambs inspected for blemishes for the purpose of offering the Tamid.
the Chamber of the Makers of the Showbread. In it they prepared the showbread.

in it the Hasmonean house hid the stones of the altar that the Greek kings had defiled. The Greek kings offered on the altar to idolatry, and when the Hasmoneans triumphed and purified the Temple, they hid the stones of the altar.
in the mesibah. A winding path.

until he reaches the immersion house. The mesibah that passed beneath the entire Temple emerged at a place on the Temple Mount outside the courtyard where there was a purification pool (the commentator on Tamid 26a).
and the length of the whole Heikhal is one hundred cubits. Above 4:4.
the altar thirty-two. Above 2:5.
the Slaughterhouse. A building with pillars topped with hooks on which they hung the sacrificial animals after slaughter, in order to flay them.
marble tables. The marble cools the meat and prevents it from spoiling (Peirush HaMishnayot, Tamid 3:5).
the pieces. The pieces of meat.
and they rinse the meat to cook it. They wash the meat being cooked before cooking it.

the place of the rings. The rings were fixed in the floor, and in them they secured the animal's legs during slaughter (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 3:5; according to Rashi, Yoma 16b, they put the animal's neck in the rings at slaughter).
and the ramp is thirty. Above 2:13.
up to the wall of the altar. The northern one.
and opposite it from the wall of the Ulam, etc.. The whole area north of the altar along its entire length from the beginning of the courtyard (in the east) to the Ulam (in the west).

it is called the north, etc.. The Torah says that the burnt offering is to be slaughtered "on the side of the altar northward" (Leviticus 1:11), and from this it is learned that the slaughter of all most-holy offerings is valid only in the north (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2-3).
the Chamber of Salt, where they put salt on the sacrifice. All sacrifices must be salted before being offered (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).

the Chamber of the Parvah, where they salt the hides of the sacred offerings. The hides of some of the offerings belong to the priests, and to prevent their spoiling they salted them in this chamber (for the reason for the chamber's name see Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 4:8).

and on its roof was an immersion house for the high priest on Yom Kippur. When the high priest changed from golden garments to white and from white to golden, he would immerse there (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 2:2-3).

the Chamber of the Rinsers, where they rinsed the innards of the sacred offerings. From the dirt of the excretions and the food not yet digested in the intestines, before they brought them up to the altar (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 6:6).
and from there a mesibah goes up, etc.. A winding ascent to the immersion pool on the roof.

half of it was holy and half non-sacred and it had two openings, etc.. Chambers built in the holy area whose opening is to the non-sacred area have the status of non-sacred (below 6:7). The Chamber of Hewn Stone was in the holy area, inside the Israelites' Courtyard, and had two openings: one to the non-sacred area and one to the holy area, and so half of it was non-sacred and half was holy (and see Pesakim VeShitot).
and in the non-sacred half the Sanhedrin sat. For it is forbidden to sit in the courtyard (below 7:6).
a well from which they fill with a wheel. By a drawing wheel.
was behind both of them. North of both of them.
and the roof of all three was level. These three chambers were adjacent to one another, and the three had a common roof.

and it is the Chamber of Pinchas the Dresser. There they stored the priestly garments. The chamber was named for the man who was in charge of the priestly garments at a certain period (see Peirush HaMishnayot, Shekalim 5:1).
and it is the Chamber of the Makers of Chavitin. There they prepared the chavitin meal offering that the high priest offered every day (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18).

and this is the form of the chambers and the whole courtyard according to its measurements. The diagram on the next page is adapted from what is drawn in the manuscripts of the Mishneh Torah. On that page are shown three-dimensional models of the Temple according to Maimonides' view and according to the view of other early authorities.
the chel. Above 5:3-4.
steps. Stairs.
the height of each step. The height of the step.
and its tread. The width (depth) of the step.
in fifteen steps. These steps were not straight but were rounded in the shape of half a threshing floor (Peirush HaMishnayot, Middot 2:5).
the platform. A raised stage on which the Levites stood and sang (below in halakhah 6).
it has three steps. One ascended to the platform by three steps, and it also served as a passage between the Israelites' Courtyard and the Priests' Courtyard.
he does not see the opening of the Heikhal. Through the gate.

so that one standing on the Mount of Anointing could see... when he sprinkles from the blood of the cow facing the Heikhal. The red heifer was slaughtered on the Mount of Olives, and from there they sprinkled from its blood toward the Heikhal (Hilchot Parah 3:2). The priest sprinkling the cow's blood had to see the Heikhal at the time he sprinkled (Hilchot Parah 4:5).
he sees the opening of the Heikhal. Over the wall above the gate.

the harps, the lyres, the cymbals and all the instruments of song. When they offered public sacrifices the Levites stood on the platform and sang. This song was accompanied by harps, flutes, lyres and cymbals (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:2-4).

if their roofs were level with the courtyard floor, their interior is non-sacred and their roofs are holy. Since the chamber's opening is toward the non-sacred area its interior is non-sacred, and since the roof is level with the height of the courtyard and is in the courtyard's area, it has the status of holy.
for the roofs and upper stories were not sanctified. When they sanctified the courtyard, they did not sanctify the roofs and upper stories (the upper floors) of the buildings in it.
most-holy offerings are not eaten there. For they must be eaten specifically in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:3).
nor are lesser-holy offerings slaughtered. For they must be slaughtered specifically in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2).

built in the non-sacred area and opening to the holy area, their interior is holy for the eating of, etc.. These chambers are considered holy only for the matter of eating sacred offerings, and by rabbinic decree they were stringent to consider them holy for all purposes (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 56a).
and one who enters there in a state of impurity is exempt. From karet and from a sacrifice, which is the law of one who enters the courtyard in a state of impurity (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:12).
the windows and the thickness of the wall. The windows in the courtyard wall, and the top of the wall.
and with Urim and Tummim. A high priest wearing the breastplate of judgment which contains the Urim and Tummim (see above 4:1 and the explanation there).

as it is said: "according to all that I...". The manner in which they sanctified the Tabernacle and its vessels is to be used for sanctification in all generations. At that time the sanctification was done according to Moses, who was a prophet and also the leader of Israel and considered a king, and Aaron, who was high priest with the Urim and Tummim, and you, the seventy elders who together with Moses served as the Sanhedrin.

they make... two thanksgiving offerings and take the leavened bread from them. The thanksgiving offering is a peace offering brought with forty loaves, thirty of the loaves made of matzah and ten loaves made of leavened bread (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot ch. 9, halakhot 5, 17-18). The thanksgiving offering and its loaves are eaten throughout Jerusalem (ibid. 10:5).
after the two thanksgiving offerings. After the leavened loaves of the two thanksgiving offerings.
and with cymbals. Cymbals.
and by the prophet's word they burn this one and eat this one. The prophet says which thanksgiving offering is to be burned and which is to be eaten.

with the remainder of the meal offering. From the meal offerings they offered a handful on the altar, and the rest of the meal offering was eaten by the priests (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 12:9). The eating of the remainder of the meal offering must be done specifically in the courtyard (ibid. 10:3).
and what Ezra did, two thanksgiving offerings. At the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem (see Nehemiah 12:27-40).
they offer all the sacrifices even though there is no house built there. See above 2:4.
and they eat lesser-holy offerings and second tithe. Which are eaten in the area within the wall of Jerusalem (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:5, Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni VeNeta Reva'i 2:1).
regarding the sabbatical year and tithes and the like. All the commandments dependent on the Land.
it did not sanctify it for the future. Rather, in the time of the Babylonian exile the sanctity ceased for them.
he did not sanctify it by conquest. For he received permission from Cyrus king of Persia to go up.

it is sanctified today even though the land was taken from them. Possession (and not conquest) sanctified it also for the future (for the nature of the difference between conquest and possession see Hilchot Terumot 1:5 and the explanation there).
in the manner we explained in Hilchot Terumah. Terumot 1:5; and see ibid. halakhah 26 that nowadays terumah and the sabbatical year are rabbinic because not all of Israel is in the Land.
and you shall not fear the Temple. One should not make the Temple itself an object of worship.
that a person should not enter the Temple Mount with his staff, etc.. This is a special law for the Temple Mount, and in a synagogue it is permitted to enter in these ways (Hilchot Tefillah 11:10).
in his apundah. A garment next to the skin that absorbs sweat. The prohibition is when he wears it without another garment over it (Peirush HaMishnayot, Berakhot 9:6).

and he should not make the Temple Mount a thoroughfare... to shorten the way... and should not enter it except for a mitzvah purpose. The same law applies to a synagogue (see Hilchot Tefillah 11:8-10).
they enter by the right and circle around and exit by the left. At every gate by which one enters the Temple Mount, one must first turn right and walk in that direction.

for I am in mourning. There are transgressions for which the transgressor is placed under a ban (for details see Hilchot Talmud Torah 6:14; for the laws of one under a ban see ibid. 7:4). One under a ban remains so until he repents and the ban is lifted for him.
and he walks on his side. In this way he can both walk and not turn his back.
the men of the mishmar. The priests serving in the Temple during a particular week (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:3).
and the men of the ma'amad. Representatives of the people of Israel who were present at the offering of the public sacrifices (ibid. 6:1-2).
and the Levites from their platform. Levites who stood on the platform in the courtyard and sang during the offering of the sacrifices (ibid. 3:3).
like one who steps backward after prayer. Hilchot Tefillah 5:10.
the Nicanor Gate because it is aligned with the Holy of Holies. Above 6:5.
in a place where he is permitted to enter. As detailed below in halakhot 15-22.
and My eyes and My heart will be there. In the Temple.
in its non-sacred half. Above 5:17.
a person is obligated to revere it as he did when it was standing. For the sanctity of the Temple was not nullified (above 6:14-15).
from Tzofim inward. Every place nearer to the Temple than Mount Scopus, on all sides.
to relieve himself. To relieve himself of his bowel needs.

and whoever urinates from Tzofim inward, etc.. One who is from Tzofim inward and faces the Holy should not urinate standing but sitting, so that he will not see the Holy while urinating, or should urinate to the sides (Bach, Orach Chaim sec. 3).
a house in the form of the Heikhal. A house in the shape of the Heikhal.
a portico in the form of the Ulam. A roofed open area before the house in the shape of the Ulam.
a courtyard corresponding to the courtyard. A courtyard exactly like the courtyard.
a menorah not of metal. Which is disqualified in the Temple (above 1:18).
three camps. Three defined areas separated from one another regarding eating sacred offerings and sending out the impure from them.
and it was four camps. The encampment of the tribes in the wilderness was divided into four camps that camped in the four directions around the Tabernacle (Numbers chapter 2).
and the camp of the Levites. The tribe of Levi camped around the Tabernacle and separated it from the camp of Israel.
and corresponding to them for the generations. Corresponding to these three camps there are three camps in the Temple and in Jerusalem.

and the chel and the Women's Courtyard are an additional degree in the House of Eternity. The chel and the Women's Courtyard are outside the courtyard, and their laws regarding sending out the impure are more stringent than the Temple Mount (below halakhot 15-16). This stringency is not because they are considered an additional camp (in the wilderness there were only three camps), but an addition that existed in the Temple.
from which the omer is brought. A meal offering made of barley that was brought with the omer offering on the sixteenth of Nisan each year (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin ch. 7, halakhot 3, 5).
and the two loaves. Leavened loaves made of wheat that were offered in the Temple on the festival of Shavuot (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 8:1-2).
and the first fruits. One of the priestly gifts, giving the first produce grown from the fruits of the seven species (Hilchot Bikkurim 2:1-2).
walled cities. For their definition see Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 12:15.
from within which they send out the lepers. Hilchot Tumat Tza'arat 10:7.
and one does not bury a dead person within them. A person who died inside the city.
the seven good men of the city. Official representatives appointed over the city's affairs.
a grave that the city surrounded. A grave that was outside the city and the city expanded to reach it.

whether from its four sides or from two sides opposite each other. To remove a grave it is not necessary that the city reach it from all directions; even if the city reached it from two parallel directions (east and west or north and south), they remove it.
more than fifty cubits. This is the distance from every city at which one must keep away all things that might harm the city or its inhabitants (Hilchot Shecheinim 10:1-3).
lesser-holy offerings and second tithe. These are eaten only in Jerusalem (Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:4-5, Ma'aser Sheni 2:1).
they do not leave a dead person overnight in it. Rather they bury him the same day (even if doing so is for his honor - Yam shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma ch. 7 sec. 44, and compare Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:8).

and they do not rent out houses within it. Jerusalem is the property of the whole people, therefore the tenants of houses in Jerusalem are not considered owners of the houses and may not collect rent for their houses.

and they do not give a place to a resident alien. A gentile who took on himself not to worship idols and to keep the commandments given to the descendants of Noah (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7). Although such a gentile is permitted to live in the Land of Israel, he is not given a residence in Jerusalem.
and they do not plant gardens and orchards in it, etc.. Because of the manure they require.
because of the creeping things. That multiply in refuse and would spread impurity when they die.
and they do not extend beams and balconies from it. Poles projecting from walls and porches. Because they might serve as a tent over corpse impurity and make the people walking beneath them impure.
and they do not make kilns in it because of the smoke. Huge ovens used for producing lime, pottery and the like, so that the smoke would not blacken the city.
and they do not raise chickens in it because of the sacred offerings. For chickens scratch in refuse and might bring dead creeping things into contact with the meat of sacred offerings.
because of the purities. Foods that must be eaten in purity, such as terumah.

and a house in it is not permanently acquired. A house sold in walled cities passes to the buyer's permanent ownership after a year. In Jerusalem this law does not apply (Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 12:12).
and it does not become impure with plagues. A house in Jerusalem that has a plague on its walls is not impure (Hilchot Tumat Tza'arat 14:11).

and it does not become a condemned city. When most of the people of a city worship idols, they are killed and the city and its property burned. Jerusalem does not become a condemned city, but its worshippers are judged as individuals who worshipped idols (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:4).

and it does not bring a broken-necked heifer. When a slain person is found on the road and it is not known who killed him, they measure the distance from him to the surrounding cities, and the elders of the nearest city bring a heifer and break its neck for atonement. If Jerusalem is in the vicinity of the slain person, they do not measure to it but to the other cities in the area (Hilchot Rotze'ach 9:4).

because it was not divided among the tribes. When the Land of Israel was divided among the various tribes, Jerusalem was not divided, and it remained the property of the whole people (this reason applies to renting houses, permanent acquisition of houses, house plagues, condemned city and broken-necked heifer).
zavim. A man from whom semen-like discharge issues without erection due to illness (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 2:1).
and zavot. A woman who sees blood outside the proper time of her menstruation (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 6:2-3).

zavim and zavot and niddot and women after childbirth. They were more stringent about their entering the Temple Mount than about one impure from a corpse, because their impurity is more severe than corpse impurity in that they make impure everything beneath their bed and seat (see also Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:3-4).
the chel. For its definition see above 5:3, and see also Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:5.
and one who had relations with a niddah. A man who had relations with a menstruating woman and became impure from her (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav UMoshav 3:1-2).
the Women's Courtyard. Above 5:7, and see also Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:6.
tevul yom. An impure person who immersed; as long as the sun has not set on him he is in a minor impurity and is forbidden to eat terumah and sacred offerings (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumah 10:1-2).
the Israelites' Courtyard is more sanctified than the Women's Courtyard. Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:7.

one lacking atonement. A zav, zavah, woman after childbirth, or leper who became pure of their impurity and have not yet brought the offering to complete their purification process, and are forbidden to eat sacred offerings (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:1).
for semikhah. Leaning the hands on the head of the offering (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:6). Semikhah is valid only in the courtyard (ibid. 3:11).
and for slaughter. The slaughter of offerings, which is valid even by non-priests (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 9:6).

and for waving. The waving of the portions of peace offerings, which is done in the courtyard by the owners together with the priest (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:6). Likewise the waving of the first fruits in the courtyard when they are brought to the Temple (Hilchot Bikkurim 3:12).

those with blemishes, those with uncut hair, and those with torn garments. All of these are forbidden to serve in the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 1:8, 1:14, 6:1). A priest who drank a revi'it of wine is also forbidden to enter between the Ulam and the altar (ibid. 1:1).
that those with... do not enter there. See ibid. 1:15.

for none enters there except with washed hands and feet. For a priest is forbidden to serve in the Temple without washing hands and feet (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 5:1), and it is entirely forbidden to enter the Heikhal not for the sake of service (ibid. 2:2).

the high priest on Yom Kippur at the time of the service. For burning the incense, sprinkling the blood of the bull and the goat, and bringing out the ladle and fire-pan of incense (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim ch. 4).
the place in the upper story aligned over the Holy of Holies. The part in the upper story of the Heikhal that was above the Holy of Holies.
once in the week. Once in seven years.
to know what needs strengthening in its repair. To check whether anything needs to be repaired there.
for impurity is set aside for the community. That when it is impossible to offer the public sacrifices in purity, they are done in impurity (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 4:9).
they enter in boxes. So that they not benefit from the sight of the Holy (above 4:13).
it is not like, etc.. Guarding honors, adorns and enlarges the house.
a palace. A palace.

you and your sons with you. Aaron the priest and his sons, and at the beginning of the verse it says "and also bring with you your brothers, the tribe of Levi, the tribe of your father," so priests and Levites.

that is, you will be guards for it, and it says "and they shall keep," etc.. The command in this passage is a command to guard the Temple, since later it says "and they shall keep the charge of the Tent of Meeting," and this verse speaks of the Levites' guarding.

and it says "and those who camp before the Tabernacle, etc.". And here the priests' guarding is stated explicitly (in this verse the root sh-m-r appears three times, and from this the Sages derived that the priests guard in three places - Peirush HaMishnayot, Tamid 1:1).
and the term "guarding" is a warning. Wherever the Torah gives a command with the root sh-m-r ("and you shall keep," "beware," etc.), it means a prohibition, a "do not."
and twenty-four watches. Groups of guards.

in Beit Avtinas. A chamber above the Water Gate, one of the southern gates of the courtyard. In this chamber they made the high priest swear on the eve of Yom Kippur that he would perform the incense service according to the tradition of the Sages (see Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:7).
and in Beit HaNitzotz. A building above the Nitzotz Gate, one of the northern gates of the courtyard.
and in Beit HaMoked. A large house in the north of the courtyard (above 5:9).
built upper stories. Raised structures.
and the archers. Guards who shoot with a bow. These guards were young priests (Peirush HaMishnayot, Tamid 1:1).
the ancestral house. The family whose turn it was to serve in the Temple on that day.
the guarding priests sleep. In each watch some of the priests slept part of the time (Mishneh LaMelekh).

opposite their heads. But not beneath their heads, since the priestly garments contain kilayim (mixed fabrics) and it is forbidden to use them other than at the time of service (Peirush HaMishnayot, Tamid 1:1, based on the Gemara).
in the mesibah. A winding path.
for the passages opening onto the Temple Mount were not sanctified. And he is permitted to walk in them while impure.
goes out and goes on his way. Since he is a tevul yom and cannot enter the courtyard and serve in the Temple that day until evening.
the five gates of the Temple Mount. Above 5:2.
that it is forbidden to sit in the courtyard. Above 7:6.
the five gates of the courtyard. Of the seven gates (above 5:4).
at the Beit HaMoked gate. The courtyard gate from Beit HaMoked (see the diagram above at the end of chapter 5).
and at the Nitzotz gate. There priests guarded in the upper story of Beit HaNitzotz (above halakhah 5).
in the Chamber of the Offering. For the animals designated for sacrifice.
and in the Chamber of the Curtain. In which they wove the curtains.
and behind the Place of Atonement. West of the Heikhal.
an appointee over all the guarding watches. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 7:4.
the officer of the Temple. He is the one in charge of the lotteries (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 6:1).
and he knocks. He knocks on the door.
the small gate. A small opening within the great gate.
took the key. Of the courtyard, from the elders of the ancestral house who slept in Beit HaMoked, in whose hands the keys of the courtyard were (above halakhah 5).
and they were examining as they went. To see that everything was in its place (Rabbi Ovadiah of Bertinoro, Tamid 1:3), or to see that there was no impurity there (Riko).
to the place of the house of the makers of chavitin. In the east of the courtyard, to the left of the Nicanor Gate (above 5:17).

and they appointed the makers of chavitin to make their chavitin. Every day they offered for the high priest the chavitin meal offering, a meal offering baked on a griddle (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:18).

except on Shabbat nights when there is no light. On Shabbat, the officer and the groups of priests who inspected the courtyard did not go with flaming torches, since it is forbidden to carry them on Shabbat, but went by lamplight.
